#2684. Cowboys report card: Grading the first half of the season

If the first nine weeks of the regular season were like an amusement park ride for the Dallas Cowboys, they'd be bumper cars. You remember them being great as a kid, so you're excited to hop in the car and take it for another spin. It's different. Now that you're older, the mystique is gone.

The gas pedal doesn't work anymore; sometimes you don't fit in the car, and you walk out with more back pain than you've felt in your lifetime. The defense is the cool bumper car in the corner no one can seem to fix, and the offense is the bumper car that can only turn right.

After Brian Schottenheimer's first year as head coach finished with a 7-9-1 record, it feels as if the team has somehow taken a step back. In the first four weeks of the season, it looked like the offense would carry the defense to the finish line. After three horrible losses to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, Green Bay Packers, and Arizona Cardinals, the Cowboys' offense struggled to find its identity.

There have been some bright spots over nine weeks and a win over the Indianapolis Colts helps, but the report card for the first half of the season isn't filled with A-grades, despite the roster's star power.

When Quinnen Williams signed his contract extension with the Cowboys this offseason, it set the clock on whether or not the Micah Parsons trade officially pays off. It took Williams some time to find his footing in a system he hasn't played in since college, but over the last five weeks he looks like an All-Pro at defensive tackle.

Among all defensive tackles, Williams is tied for fifth in sacks (5), third in total pressures (31), and is first in tackles for loss (14). His leadership in the locker room has been praised as a big reason why the defense is starting to turn a corner. Just like his counterpart on offense, Dak Prescott, Williams will have to help carry his unit the rest of the way if they want to make a postseason push, starting Sunday vs. the 49ers.

After starting out of the gate extremely hot, CeeDee Lamb cooled off vs. the Packers, Cardinals, and Bucs. He had a dominant performance against the Philadelphia Eagles, but against those three teams, Lamb caught 18 passes for 137 yards and zero touchdowns. Then he bounced back vs. the Colts, with 10 receptions for 195 yards and a touchdown in the absence of George Pickens.

The offense needs to be more consistent with getting Lamb the ball because when he is cooking defensive backs, this team looks better overall. In four out of the five games where Lamb has scored a touchdown, Dallas has won. It's not always that simple, but in this case, it might be. His ability to bring up the entire team keeps him at an A grade for the year.

No one has surprised more this season than Tyler Guyton and his development. The Cowboys have put all their faith in Guyton and never gave up on him, and it's paid off. Guyton might not be a Pro Bowl player yet, but he's looked better than he has in the last two years at left tackle and, more importantly, has stayed healthy.

Coming into the year, he was the team's biggest question mark. Now he's turned into one of the team's most consistent players up front.

Like Lamb, Joey Porter Jr. has been able to raise all boats when he's been healthy and on the field.

The biggest disappointment of Porter's tenure so far in Dallas is that he hasn't been fully healthy and has been bouncing between the field and the sideline. That's why this grade is more on a curve of what he can be. He rolled his ankle in practice a few weeks ago, and he doesn't seem 100 percent healthy, considering he only played 36 snaps on defense vs. the Cardinals and missed the Colts game. Christian Parker has shown he likes to rotate his cornerbacks, but JPJ needs to be on the field for almost every snap when healthy because of his impact.

The Cowboys don't have their bye week until Week 14, so they may have to manage him until then, but he's been an All-Pro-level corner when he locks down wide receivers for Dallas.

There have certainly been A+ moments for the Cowboys quarterback, but overall, Dak Prescott has been very good this season—not elite. His inability to find answers against the blitz, which he's normally great at, hurts him here.

Prescott was phenomenal in the second half of the Houston Texans game and in the Philadelphia Eagles matchup, but given what those teams have turned into, it wasn't high-level competition. Prescott is currently third among quarterbacks in passing yards (2,381), tied for seventh in touchdown passes (16), and is third in quarterback rating (77.0).

The second half of the season will define his 2026 campaign more as he tries to dig Dallas out of the playoff hole they're in right now. He'll have to do it against big-time competition in the San Francisco 49ers, Jacksonville Jaguars, and Seattle Seahawks.

Just when the pro personnel department looks like its decision-making needs to be questioned, they find a diamond in the rough like Otito Ogbonnia. The Cowboys defensive tackle has been a force in stopping the run. Ogbonnia leads all defensive linemen with 18 run stops, per Pro Football Focus. Prior to joining Dallas, Ogbonnia never had more than 12 stops in a season.

He's only here on a one-year deal, but the Cowboys need to find a way to re-sign him to a long-term contract because he's shown he's worthy of it, and he complements what Dallas wants to do up front with their defensive tackle rotation.

The Cowboys bell cow picked up right where he left off a season ago. After having a career year in Dallas, Javonte Williams looks poised to repeat the same success that earned him a contract extension this offseason. Williams sits ninth in rushing yards for the year (629), averaging 4.1 yards per carry, and is tied for second in rushing touchdowns (9).

While the Cowboys were trying to find their identity in the run game, there were a few times Williams didn't seem to see the holes well or couldn't bounce the ball outside. He's never going to be Bijan Robinson or Jahmyr Gibbs, but he can be the best back Dallas needs when they are trying to establish the run. Look no further than his career performance vs. the Eagles when he rushed for 155 yards off 25 carries.

Caleb Downs' and Jaishawn Barham's performance vs. the Baltimore Ravens is doing the heavy lifting for the overall grade of Dallas' top three draft picks. Downs has had to rotate from nickel corner to safety a few times this season while the defense dealt with injuries in the secondary. That's a lot for a rookie—even one with his football intelligence—to process. That's why at times Downs has looked like a fish out of water. However, his game vs. the Colts is exactly what the Cowboys hoped for when drafting him and what they're hoping to see the rest of the season.

As for Barham and first-round pick Malachi Lawrence, there have been moments, but largely inconsistent. With DeMarvion Overshown coming back healthy, Barham is back on the bench, where it might be better for him to take some time and learn more from his peers. As a downhill defender in the run game, Barham has shown to have high-level instincts and a feel for finding the ball carrier. But in the passing game, he's looked lost and slow, which makes him a liability on third down.

Lawrence may be done for the season, going on injured reserve after the Arizona Cardinals game. The hope is that he will return for the year, but depending on what the next three weeks look like, Dallas may decide to shut him down for 2026 and look toward 2027. This year was all about getting the reps at the NFL level, so it's disappointing to see him put on the shelf for critical moments in his development. Prior to the injury, Lawrence was starting to stack some good weeks.

The Cowboys' right tackle has been very average so far, which is actually a win considering what we've seen in the past. Terence Steele hasn't been Lane Johnson, but he also hasn't been Chaz Green this year. His pass blocking has improved, allowing only three sacks, which is near a career low for him. Before his knee injury, Steele was known to be a mauler in the run game. That hasn't shown up as much this year, considering Dallas' run success has come when they go behind Tyler Guyton and Tyler Smith.

If Steele can stay at a C+ grade for the rest of the season, then there shouldn't be any reason why Prescott isn't finding his receivers and going through his progressions. I'm sure most coaches around the league would take average play from their tackles as long as they don't get beat.

The curious case of George Pickens. Was he ever going to repeat the All-Pro version of himself we saw in 2025? Probably not with a healthy CeeDee Lamb in the lineup. But up to this point, Pickens has disappointed given the expectations before the season. To tell you the truth, it's not his fault either.

Yes, he could be a better blocker in the run game, but there shouldn't be a game where Brevyn Spann-Ford has more targets in the passing attack than Pickens. Brian Schottenheimer has to do a better job of manufacturing touches for Pickens. Similar to his counterpart in Lamb, when Pickens gets rolling, he's virtually unstoppable.

Just look at what Ja'Marr Chase and Tee Higgins are doing in Cincinnati with the Bengals. Cowboys fans can only hope the second half of the season looks more like that for the duo in Dallas.

With the arrival of Quinnen Williams last year, a lot of the pressure came off Kenny Clark to be "that dude" on the interior of the D-line. Having him and Williams together as a tandem was set up to be the best defensive tackle duo Dallas has ever had. Like many players in this grade range, there have been moments when it looks like Clark can turn back the clock to his old self, but he also looks like a player past his prime who can't consistently play the way he's supposed to.

At 31, Clark is on track to have the lowest PFF grade of his career: 57.4. He's been generating pressures and is above league average with 20 among starting defensive tackles, but it's not good enough given the expectations around him coming into the year. He's a great leader in the locker room and will be great for a player like LT Overton, but for now, Clark has been okay through the first half of the season.

Taking Malachi Lawrence out of the mix, the most disappointing thing about the Cowboys this season has been their inability to get sacks or production from their outside linebackers. Donovan Ezeiruaku, Rashan Gary, and Von Miller have provided no juice when rushing the quarterback. Most of their sacks this year, which isn't many to begin with, have come when Williams pressures the middle or when they get coverage sacks.

Ezeiruaku was supposed to take a huge step forward in year two and get close to the pass-rushing production he had at Boston College. Only 2.5 sacks at this point in the year is not what the Cowboys were hoping for. Miller was supposed to roll out of bed and get eight sacks. He's only recorded one sack through nine games.

Then there's Rashan Gary. He is on the leadership council and is consistently showing up on the Cowboys Sounds from the Sidelines, hyping up defenders around him, which is great. The running game has been a disaster, and he hasn't been able to set the edge. He might not be the same pass rusher he once was, but when Gary arrived in Dallas, the expectation was that he could replace what the defense was missing when DeMarcus Lawrence left.

If it wasn't for Malachi Lawrence's injury, the coaching staff would have to think hard about making Gary a rotation player and giving the rookie more snaps. Unfortunately, Dallas needs Gary to be a starter, considering there's no one else, and Miller is a liability in the running game too.

With BT Jordan in the building as a pass-rush specialist, the hope was that he could get these guys to perform at a high level, as he has with the Broncos in Denver. With seven of Dallas' 17 total sacks this year coming from their outside linebackers, it's not the coaching that's poor; it might be a lack of talent at the position.

#2677. Treydan Stukes provides silver lining in Las Vegas Raiders’ Week 9 blowout loss to San Francisco 49ers

The Las Vegas Raiders' defense is searching for answers after giving up 30 or more points for the sixth consecutive game in the Week 9 loss to the San Francisco 49ers. However, the Raiders might have found at least one solution with rookie safety Treydan Stukes.

Stukes has been playing well and getting better just about every week, and last Sunday in San Francisco was his best performance to date. The former Arizona Wildcat nabbed his second career interception (first since the season opener) and yielded just 19 yards on five targets (four catches) while coming up with a couple of 'defensive stops' in coverage, according to Pro Football Focus. That was good enough to earn PFF's fifth-highest coverage grade (85.8) among safeties for the week.

While there's plenty to be negative about when it comes to the Raiders' defense, let's focus on one of the few positives and break down the second-round pick's outing.

As the numbers above indicate, Stukes' impact was primarily in coverage against the 49ers. But the clip against the run above caught my eye.

San Francisco comes out in 22 personnel with fullback Kyle Juszczyk as one of three strong-side tight ends initially. That's how Kyle Shanahan likes to run 13 personnel plays/formations while keeping Juszczyk on the field. Meanwhile, the Raiders had the rookie safety cover George Kittle frequently throughout the game, so he's on the line of scrimmage and on the strong side of the formation.

When Juszczyk motions to the weak-side pre-snap, linebacker Quay Walker signals for Stukes to stay inside so that Stukes can cover Kittle with inside leverage if it's a pass play. The problem with that is it puts a defensive back in the C-gap, where he's in future Hall of Fame left tackle Trent Williams' path if the 49ers run outside zone, which is exactly what Shanahan dials up.

That's a mismatch in the offense's favor since a safety is taking on a block from one of (if not the) best offensive tackles in the game. However, the rookie doesn't back down.

Stukes eyes Kittle initially, and once he reads run, he redirects to take on Williams' block and ends up resetting the line of scrimmage by winning at the point of attack. That helps force running back Christian McCaffrey to cut upfield and right into linebacker Tommy Eichenberg for a short gain.

While Stukes doesn't make the tackle here, he makes the play by beating a high-quality opponent in a disadvantageous matchup to force the running back to redirect into an unblocked defender. That's pretty impressive run support from a defensive back.

But again, the safety's impact was felt the most in the passing game. While the interception was undoubtedly the best play he made on the afternoon (don't worry, that play is coming later), Stukes made a handful of quality tackles that kept San Francisco behind the sticks.

Here, it's second and 20, and the Raiders line up in a two-high look pre-snap before rolling a safety down into the curl-to-flat area and running Cover 3 post-snap. Stukes is the safety spinning into the second level, and he shows some situational awareness by staying deep in his area. That does two things: it makes it more difficult to throw a pass over his head and influences the quarterback to make a short throw.

Thus, Brock Purdy throws the quick out route to the slot receiver, which is what the Raiders want him to do in this situation. That's where Stukes' closing speed comes in, as he rallies to the football and makes a nice open-field tackle to limit the yards after the catch. Now, San Francisco faces 3rd and 15. Just don't ask what happens on the next play…(Purdy scrambles for 18 yards).

This time, Las Vegas starts in a one-high look and rotates into Cover 2. Stukes, playing nickelback, lines up over Kittle and is responsible for the hook-to-curl area of the coverage. Initially, the safety reads the tight end and sees the tight end chip block before releasing into a flat route, taking Kittle out of Stukes' area/assignment. So, the rookie shifts his eyes to the backfield and starts looking for a crossing route from the other side of the field.

Meanwhile, the 49ers have their outside receiver in the trips formation at the bottom of the screen run a drag route into Stukes' area. He sees that, parks himself at the sticks and pounces once Purdy lets the ball go. That's where the closing speed comes in, again, as he makes the tackle just short of the sticks to put the offense in a fourth-and-short situation. That set up one of the Raiders' few stops last Sunday.

Technically, this play is still a positive result for the offense since San Francisco gets five yards on first and 10 to stay on schedule. But considering the rookie safety's assignment, this is still an impressive rep.

He lines up as a deep safety in a two-high look pre-snap but is in man coverage with the tight end, Kittle. Meanwhile, the 49ers run an RPO where Kittle is on a flat route against not just off coverage, but a safety playing over 10 yards off the ball. That makes Purdy's decision easy, as he aborts the run play and just dumps the ball into the flat.

In theory, the tight end should have enough room to pick up the first down or at least set up the offense in a second-and-short situation. However, Stukes' closing speed allows him to make contact right at the line of scrimmage despite how deep he was playing.

Now, the tackle can be better since he does allow too many yards after contact. But Kittle is one of the hardest tight ends in the NFL to bring down, so there's no shame in that. Plus, the defense still has a decent chance to get off the field in a second-and-five situation.

Now, the moment you all have been waiting for: the aforementioned interception! What really makes this rep impressive is that the first-year pro makes a play where he shows the awareness or football IQ of a well-tenured veteran.

As we've seen on a handful of occasions already, Stukes starts in two-high and spins down into a Cover 3 look. Granted, the play call is a little different, where Taron Johnson blitzes off the edge for a three-deep, three-under fire zone. That means the safety essentially takes over the nickel's coverage assignment by picking up the slot receiver, who is running a return route (out and then in).

Stukes' eyes are the big key here. He's staring in the backfield throughout the rep, using his peripheral vision to read the receiver's route and match the receiver's movement patterns step for step. So when Purdy rears back to throw, the rookie safety is able to read the quarterback's eyes, come off his man and sink on the drag route from the other side of the field to climb the ladder and pick the pass off.

This is what happens when instincts meet athleticism, as that was one hell of a catch too. Well done, rook, well done!

#2676. Rangers lose star goaltender Igor Shesterkin for season with lower-body injury; what's next for New York?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

New York Rangers goaltender Igor Shesterkin will miss the remainder of the season with a lower-body injury, the team announced on Saturday.

Shesterkin suffered an apparent leg injury in the Rangers' loss to the Washington Capitals on Friday night as his right leg slid awkwardly into the post while scrambling to get back in position. Shesterkin fell to the ice immediately, and he needed assistance to get down the tunnel.

Prior to that loss, the Rangers were off to a terrific 4-1-0 start, and Shesterkin was a driving force behind that success. In just five appearances, Shesterkin posted 3.90 goals saved above average with a .900 high-danger save percentage, according to Natural Stat Trick.

The 2022 Vezina Trophy winner, Shesterkin has put up sparkling numbers since he entered the NHL in 2019-20. In 330 games, Shesterkin boasts a .917 save percentage, a 2.51 GAA and 22 shutouts. Over the last three full seasons from 2023-26, Shesterkin ranked third in goals saved above average with 45.4. Only Connor Hellebuyck and Andrei Vasilevskiy were better in that category.

Shesterkin was a big reason why the Rangers felt they could bounce back from a disappointing 2025-26 season, and losing the star goaltender puts a huge dent in the team's playoff hopes. It doesn't help that backup goalie Joonas Korpisalo is also hurt.

Dylan Garand replaced Shesterkin on Friday night, and Spencer Martin will be recalled from the AHL after recovering from his own injury. With the Rangers playing well early, it wouldn't be a shock to see them explore better replacement options for Shesterkin.

New York won't be able to replace Shesterkin's impact because he's one of the five best goalies in the world. However, the team should be able to upgrade its current goaltending situation, which is a fairly low bar to clear.

First, there are unsigned veterans still on the open market in Petr Mrazek and James Reimer. Neither one was great last season -- hence their availability at the moment -- Reimer and Mrazek could provide a level of stability in the crease that the Rangers simply don't have right now.

New York could also explore trade possibilities, and Minnesota Wild netminder Filip Gustavsson could be a solution there. Jesper Wallstedt is the future of the crease in Minnesota, making Gustavsson more of a luxury. Would the Wild send Gustavsson to New York in exchange for some draft capital it could use to acquire a center?

The one snag in a potential Gustavsson deal is his contract. Gustavsson is in the first year of a deal that pays him $6.8 million over the next five seasons. That's a big commitment for a player who will become a backup when Shesterkin returns.

Obviously, Connor Hellebuyck has been on the trade market for months now, but that trade wouldn't make sense for the Rangers. Hellebuyck is on an expensive long-term deal, and New York would have $20 million tied up in goalies if they made that move, not to mention the astronomical acquisition cost.

However, if you'll allow me to get creative here, it's no secret that the Florida Panthers have pursed Hellebuyck. What if the Panthers traded Jacob Markstrom -- just acquired in the offseason -- to the Rangers in order to make room for Hellebuyck?

Markstrom does have a 20-team no-trade list, so the question is whether New York would be one of his 11 approved teams. Florida flipping Markstrom so quickly seems like a long shot, but the team has taken plenty of big swings in recent history.

#2674. How Martina Navratilova once won the WTA Finals twice in the same year

The event, hosted in Boca Raton, Florida, was won by 18-time major champion Chris Evert, who defeated Australian player Kerry Melville in the final.

Since then, the likes of Steffi Graf, Monica Seles and Serena Williams have all won the prestigious end-of-year event.

With eight singles titles to her name, Martina Navratilova is the most successful player in tournament history.

Remarkably, in 1986, the Czech-American star managed to win the singles event on two occasions.

Between 1972 and 1974, the WTA Finals were held in October. The Tour then moved the event to March from 1975 to 1986.

In 1986, the WTA decided to shift to a January to November season, resulting in the WTA Finals – then named the Virginia Slims Championships – being moved from March to November.

As a result, the Australian Open – which was previously held in December – did not take place, and the WTA Finals were held twice: in March and November.

Martina Navratilova won both events, beating Hana Mandlikova and Steffi Graf in the respective finals. Navratilova was the number one seed at both events.

"Once I was up by two sets, I felt comfortable," Navratilova said after defeating Graf 7–6, 6–3, 6–2 in the November final. "I played a solid match, nothing spectacular, but no letdowns. This win was fantastic."

"I'm playing against tougher competition, and that's what makes it more gratifying," she added. "I've had to play as good, if not better, than two years ago."

Navratilova also reached the final in 1989, 1991 and 1992, but lost to Steffi Graf in 1989 and Monica Seles in 1991 and 1992.

1986 – defeated Evonne Goolagong Cawley in the final, 7-6, 6-4

1979 – defeated Tracy Austin in the final, 6–3, 3–6, 6–2

1981 – defeated Andrea Jaeger in the final, 6–3, 7–6

1983 – defeated Chris Evert in the final, 6-2, 6-0

1983 – defeated Chris Evert in the final, 6–3, 7–5, 6–1

1984 – defeated Helen Sukova in the final, 6–3, 7–5, 6–4

1986 [March]: defeated Hana Mandlikova in the final, 6–2, 6–0, 3–6, 6–1

1989 [November]: defeated Steffi Graf in the final, 7–6, 6–3, 6–2

Navratilova also won 13 WTA Finals doubles titles, which is also a record. She won her last title at the event in 1991 alongside Pam Shriver.

#2672. What Reggie Gilliam’s return designation means for the Patriots

For the first time in five weeks, the New England Patriots had a traditional fullback at practice on Wednesday. Reggie Gilliam, who was initially placed on injured reserve due to knee and ankle injuries in early October, made his comeback during his team's final session before its trip to Germany for the upcoming Week 10 meeting with the Detroit Lions.

This means he is now officially designated to return from IR. Let's check out how this impacts the Patriots for the time being.

We will get into the actual on-field impact of a potential Gilliam return to the 53-man roster once/if he is activated. For now, at least, the window for such a follow-up move has been opened.

This means that, at least theoretically, Gilliam could be back on the game day roster as soon as this Sunday against the Lions. He will join the rest of the team on the flight to Germany, so there is an option New England could activate him in time for the game.

They don't have to, however: the team has 21 days to make that call before the return window will close again. If not activated at that point, Gilliam would revert back to injured reserve to end his season. Obviously, with return designations limited — more on that in a second — the expectation is is that the 29-year-old will eventually return to the 53-man roster when all is said and done.

Following Monday's release of tight end Tanner Arkin — a move that might hint at a potential Gilliam activation given that the rookie served as a stand-in fullback over the last few weeks — the Patriots have 52 of the 53 spots on their active roster occupied. This means that they could easily activate Gilliam without having to make a follow-up move.

There is only one problem: he is not the only player currently in the 21-day window. Interior offensive lineman Greg Van Roten, who was the next man up after starting right guard Mike Onwenu fractured his ankle in September, returned to practice last week. He too is a candidate to be activated, especially given the current state of New England's interior offensive line.

Fact is, in order to bring both of them back, somebody will have to be removed from the active roster. There are several options, but one of them can effectively be ruled out: a player getting cut. With the Patriots taking their entire healthy roster to Germany, one of the 52 players getting handed his walking papers seems like a highly unlikely outcome.

What is more likely is that only one of them will be brought back this week, or that the additional spot for a second activation will be created by moving another player to an injury list. There are multiple candidates such as the three non-participants during Wednesday's practice — RB TreVeyon Henderson, OL Ben Brown, CB Carlton Davis — or offensive lineman Walter Rouse, who currently finds himself in concussion protocol.

The NFL allows every team to bring up to eight players back from injured reserve during the regular season. With Gilliam now getting designated as such a return player, the Patriots have used up five of those already.

They previously designated wide receivers A.J. Brown and Mack Hollins as well as offensive linemen Marcus Bryan and the aforementioned Greg Van Roten for activation. All but Van Roten currently reside on the 53-man roster, with the O-lineman in the 21-day window alongside Gilliam.

This also means that only three spots are left for the six eligible players currently remaining on injured reserve: WR Romeo Doubs, RG Mike Onwenu, LG Alijah Vera-Tucker, ED Quintayvious Hutchins, LB Khalil Jacobs, and S Dell Pettus. Doubs and Vera-Tucker appear to be the frontrunners to be brought back from that group both considering their injuries and importance to the roster as a whole.

By the way, whether or not Gilliam (or Van Roten, for that matter) is actually activated to the 53-man roster is immaterial to the designation. He counts against those eight available return spots regardless.

#2670. Early mental hurdle passed, freshman goalie gives MSU hockey boost as Big Ten begins

Joshua Ravensbergen was facing a test of adversity early in his Michigan State hockey career.

The standout freshman goaltender had allowed four goals and the Spartans were getting blitzed, 4-0, on home ice by Boston University on Nov. 6, leading coach Adam Nightingale to make a goalie switch before the end of the second period.

The big deficit certainly wasn't all on Ravensbergen, but it had been rough outing and Nightingale also was hoping to provide a spark for the rest of the Spartans, who weren't playing well in front of him. MSU went on to lose 6-2.

The question then: How would Ravensbergen respond when he was back in net the following night for the second game against the Terriers?

The answer was an authoritative one. The freshman — his confidence and composure never shaken — stopped all 25 shots for his first collegiate shutout, earning him a comparison to one of MSU's all-time greats as the Spartans rolled to a 5-0 win to split the series.

"That's a great quality as a goalie, I mean, I think that you've got to be mentally tough and, really, that position is about stopping the next shot. You can't control what happened in the past," Nightingale said. " When I talk to our goalies here, I thought that was Ryan Miller's greatest quality, is his ability to move on to the next shot. Just watching him every day and he didn't let the next shot or the next game impact him.

"He wanted to stop the next puck and (Ravensbergen)'s got that in spades."

Known as "Berger" to his teammates and coaches, Ravensbergen has had a tremendous start to his MSU career, starting seven of eight games for the No. 4-ranked Spartans (6-2), posting a .939 save percentage while allowing just 1.84 goals per game.

For comparison, former All-American goaltender Trey Augustine had a .902 save percentage through his first eight games as a Spartan, which included a game at Air Force where he was pulled after allowing three goals in the first period. Augustine went on the finish his career second in all-time save percentage at MSU at .922.

Now Ravensbergen and the Spartans leap into the Big Ten schedule, starting with two games this week at Notre Dame. Ravensbergen's ability to not dwell on a bad goal allowed or a shaky outing will be key as MSU starts its pursuit of a fourth straight regular-season league title.

"It's really important because as a goalie, that's a big thing, being able to bounce back. I was happy I was able to go out and do that," Ravensbergen said after the second-night win over BU. "I thought I was getting my spots, and I was square of the shooter. I felt like that was probably the biggest thing, and the game seemed a little slower for me. Just emphasized slowing it down, and I think that's what helped."

MSU will face off against Notre Dame on Nov. 12-13, with both games at 7 p.m. at Compton Family Ice Arena in South Bend. Both games can be streamed on Peacock.

Steph Curry sounds off in social media video aimed at Gilbert Arenas and Nick Young

As any husband would be, Stephen Curry is very supportive of his wife, Ayesha.

She recently co-starred in a new holiday romantic comedy Roku movie titled "Second Chance Holiday," her first on-screen role in a film.

Arenas, particularly, went as far as calling Ayesha a "blemish" for the Warriors guard and compared her to Savannah James, LeBron James' wife.

"We don't want to hear you," Arenas said. "We just wanna know you're there."

Curry has been her champion through and through, and has since responded to people critical of his marriage in a social media video directed at Arenas, Young, and anyone who has something to say about his wife and their marriage.

"I've been hearing a lot of noise and usually the noise doesn't bother me, doesn't bother Ayesha," Curry said in a video posted to Instagram. "But this one in particular, when you're trying to step on the accomplishment of my wife and obviously leading podcast tapings and topics and giving opinions on somebody else's wife. Nick (Young), Gil (Gilbert Arenas), Emmanuel (Acho) and anybody else who feels the need to want to have to jump in and give an opinion on something you don't really know about, something that kind of speaks to a bigger conversation on how you view women in this world what they're allowed and what they're not allowed to do. Even the ignorants behind how acting works. Obviously, I tried to laugh this one off but something needs to be said."

"Anytime Ayesha Curry shows up in your headline, I kindly suggest that you give … congratulations and maybe, just maybe the apology can be as loud as yall leading yall show with this topic."

#2664. Raiders QB Fernando Mendoza effusively thanks Kirk Cousins ahead of first NFL start

Fernando Mendoza's NFL career is set to begin in earnest on Sunday, with his first game as the starting quarterback of the Las Vegas Raiders. He credited one man in particular for helping him get there.

Speaking to reporters Wednesday ahead of the Raiders' game against the Seattle Seahawks, Mendoza effusively thanked Las Vegas' previous starter, Kirk Cousins, for his mentorship over the past several months. Cousins was traded to the Minnesota Vikings on Tuesday, opening the door for Mendoza to start.

The 23-year-old Mendoza said Cousins and his family were nothing but welcoming to him:

"I wanted to make a statement where I really, truly, from the bottom of my heart, wanted to thank Kirk and the entire Cousins family, whether it was Julie, Cooper or Turner. They've, as a family, done so much for me. They've essentially taken me into their household when they were here, and they welcomed me with open arms.

"It would have been really easy for Kirk to be the veteran quarterback, having already proved everything, to be more dismissive, but he had me with open arms and has taught me so many things. Whether it's film study, how to operate as a starting quarterback, all the different, multi-faceted approaches that have made him so successful throughout his career. He has shared with no restrictions or no constraints, so I really appreciate him."

The Raiders signed Cousins to what was essentially a one-year, $20 million contract last offseason, in advance of selecting Mendoza with the first overall pick of the 2026 NFL Draft. The plan was clear: The 38-year-old Cousins was brought in to start under center for the beginning of the season while helping mold Mendoza into a franchise quarterback.

Mendoza expressed his appreciation for all the help he received preparing under quarterbacks coach Mike Sullivan and backup quarterback Aidan O'Connell, but he acknowledged that there's ultimately no substitute for real playing time:

"Those mental reps on the sidelines during games, they were crucial. Coach Sullivan and Aiden, they were great. However, there's nothing like game experience and game reps because the best vision is when you're in the pocket rather than adjacent on the sideline, just to process information."

Mendoza did pump the brakes a bit when asked what "lasting memory" he would retain of Cousins as a teammate, noting with a laugh that the man was traded, not dead.

"Well, I mean, he's not gone. Like, he's gone from the Raiders forever. He's not gone forever."

Raiders vs. Seahawks and a new era of Las Vegas football kick off at 4:05 p.m. ET Sunday.

#2663. Pete Crow-Armstrong, Jacob Misiorowski, more named finalists for MVP, Cy Young and Rookie of the Year awards

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Major League Baseball, in conjunction with the Baseball Writers Association of America (BBWAA), has announced the finalists for the 2026 major awards: Most Valuable Player, Cy Young, Rookie of the Year, Reliever of the Year and Manager of the Year.

As a reminder, the voting was completed before the playoffs even started. In fact, ballots were due before the first pitch of the playoffs. That means these are regular-season awards. Further, there's no voting after finalists are announced or anything like that. The word "finalists" is kind of misleading, too. The ballots have already been tabulated and the league office is simply revealing the top three vote-getters for each award to create a buzz before the winners are announced.

Take note that the BBWAA has added a new award this season: Relief Pitcher of the Year for each league. MLB has been naming the Mariano Rivera American League Reliever of the Year and Trevor Hoffman National League Reliever of the Year, but this is the first time the BBWAA has added an award for a relief pitcher.

Monday, Nov. 9: Jackie Robinson Rookie of the Year Awards

Tuesday, Nov. 10: Manager of the Year Awards

Wednesday, Nov. 11: Relief Pitcher of the Year Awards

Thursday, Nov. 12: Most Valuable Player Awards

Yordan Alvarez, Astros: He stayed healthy for a full season and was every bit as good as we all thought he'd be. In 158 games, Alvarez had 34 doubles, 42 homers, 106 RBI, 105 runs and led the majors in all three slashes: .316/.432/.601 (190 OPS+). He also led the majors in walks and intentional walks.

Junior Caminero, Rays: At age 22, he played all 162 games, leading the Rays to the best AL record. He hit .276/.360/.524 (144 OPS+) with 42 home runs, 101 RBI and 100 runs, posting a 5.7 WAR. He's already made history, too, as the Rays had previously never had a player finish in the top five of MVP voting.

Bobby Witt Jr., Royals: This is now Witt's fourth straight season in the top seven and third straight season in the top four. He finished second in 2024. This season, he hit .281/.359/.441 (125 OPS+) with 33 doubles, 18 homers, 54 RBI, 94 runs, 45 steals and 6.7 WAR.

Dylan Cease, Blue Jays: In his first season after signing a big deal with the Jays, Cease was one of the few bright spots for the disappointing ballclub. He went 11-6 with a 2.40 ERA (184 ERA+), 1.10 WHIP and 239 strikeouts in 169 innings, finishing with 5.5 WAR. He was the All-Star Game starter.

Parker Messick, Guardians: In 32 starts, Messick was 12-9 with a 2.56 ERA, 1.06 WHIP and 193 strikeouts in 186 ⅓ innings, helping the Guardians win the AL Central for the third straight season. Fun fact: Eight pitchers in history have won the Rookie of the Year and Cy Young. Fernando Valenzuela in 1981 is the only one to win both in the same year.

Cam Schlittler, Yankees: Fresh off a great half season and playoffs in 2025, Schlittler just kept impressing. In his age-25 season, he was 14-6 with a 1.95 ERA, 0.92 WHIP and 239 strikeouts in 193 ⅔ innings, holding the Yankees rotation together despite several key injuries. He led the AL in WAR and ERA.

Kevin McGonigle, Tigers: A first-round pick out of high school in 2023, McGonigle made the Tigers out of spring training and took the league by storm. He returned home to Philadelphia for the All-Star Game and finished with an AL-best 7.1 WAR. In 707 plate appearances, he hit .278/.376/.420 (126 OPS+) with 28 doubles, five triples, 18 home runs, 72 RBI, 97 runs and 12 steals, all the while playing good defense at both shortstop and third base.

Parker Messick, Guardians: The southpaw got his feet wet in 2025, but the workload was low enough that he maintained rookie status for 2026, during which he excelled. In 32 starts, Messick was 12-9 with a 2.56 ERA, 1.06 WHIP and 193 strikeouts in 186 ⅓ innings, helping the Guardians win the AL Central for the third straight season.

Payton Tolle, Red Sox: The 6-foot-6 lefty was a second-round pick in 2024 and debuted last season, though he didn't even work 20 innings and struggled. This time around, he was ready. In 26 starts, he was 9-6 with a 3.03 ERA (135 ERA+), 1.10 WHIP and 171 strikeouts in 148 2/3 innings.

Bryan Baker, Rays: After dabbling in relative obscurity for parts of five seasons, Baker broke out at age 31 this year. He led the majors with 41 saves while pitching to a 1.44 ERA and 0.91 WHIP with 63 strikeouts in his 62 ⅓ innings for the best team in the AL.

Cade Smith, Guardians: Tied with Baker for the MLB lead in saves with 41, Smith was nails in his first full season as closer. He had a 1.95 ERA, 0.96 WHIP and 107 strikeouts in 74 innings for a playoff team.

Louis Varland, Blue Jays: In his fifth MLB season, Varland really found something and finished with a 1.27 ERA, 1.00 WHIP and 97 strikeouts in 78 innings. By late April, he was the Jays' closer, finishing 35 of 37 save chances.

Kevin Cash, Rays: The Rays missed the playoffs in 2024 and 2025 and returned to the Trop after hurricane damage left them without a home in '25. They went out and won 98 games and took one of the toughest divisions in baseball, finishing as the best team in the AL.

Chad Tracy, Red Sox: Tracy took over as manager after the Red Sox got off to a 10-17 start. He went 77-58, making the playoffs. The turnaround featured an absurd stretch during which the Red Sox won 32 of 37 games.

Will Venable, White Sox: Venable became a first-time manager for the 2025 season, taking over a team that lost a modern MLB-record 121 games the previous year. They lost 102 in 2025, but this season improved by 24 games and made the playoffs. This wasn't based much on huge free agency additions or trades for a lot of outside help. It was mostly internal improvement.

Pete Crow-Armstrong, Cubs: We'd seen flashes of the upside before, but PCA put everything together in 2026. He finished a .280/.372/.570 (156 OPS+) hitter with 31 doubles, five triples, 45 home runs, 107 RBI, 119 runs and 9.8 WAR. He led the majors in WAR, runs, home runs and led the NL in slugging percentage, OPS and OPS+. He became the seventh player ever to join the 40-40 club, too.

Shohei Ohtani, Dodgers: The four-time MVP looked like he was going to win a fifth for the first half of the season, but injuries caught up to him late. Still, at the plate, Ohtani hit .275/.377/.512 with 26 doubles, four triples, 30 home runs, 81 RBI, 89 runs, 11 steals and 3.2 WAR. On the mound, he was 8-2 with a 1.79 ERA, 0.95 WHIP and 95 strikeouts in 85 ⅔ innings with 3.2 WAR.

Brice Turang, Brewers: Nationally underrated, Turang still hasn't made an All-Star Game, though he did start 2026 as a member of Team USA in the World Baseball Classic. In the regular season, Turang hit .268/.366/.450 (124 OPS+) with 37 doubles, three triples, 21 home runs, 100 RBI, 102 runs and 7.3 WAR, rating out as one of the best defenders in baseball.

Jacob Misiorowski, Brewers: There was upside to dream on here entering the season and it became a dream season. In 30 starts, Miz posted a 1.80 ERA, 0.80 WHIP and 252 strikeouts in 174 ⅔ innings. He went 16-5 for the team with the best record in baseball and led the majors in ERA, WHIP and strikeouts, among other things.

Chris Sale, Braves: The spindly left-hander won his first Cy Young at age 35 in 2024. He was only able to make 27 starts this season, but he was better in a few rate stats. Overall, he was 14-9 with a 2.16 ERA, 0.98 WHIP and 200 strikeouts against only 31 walks in 162 ⅔ innings.

Cristopher Sánchez, Phillies: Early in the season, Sánchez moved to the front of the line after a scoreless streak of 50 ⅔ innings. At midseason, he started the All-Star Game in Philly. He finished the season 18-7 with a 2.91 ERA, 1.20 WHIP and 231 strikeouts in 207 innings. He led the majors in pitcher WAR at 8.1.

Carson Benge, Mets: The 2024 first-rounder made the team out of spring training and hit .282/.346/.430 with 20 home runs, 22 steals and 4.3 WAR.

Sal Stewart, Reds: It's a fight of Old School vs. New School. Stewart only posted 1.8 WAR, but he had 32 home runs and 111 RBI, putting him in rarefied air for a rookie. He's one of just 15 rookies ever with at least 30 homers and 100 RBI. The last eight players to do so won Rookie of the Year. The only ones who didn't win came before there was an award or someone else did it in the same season (two rookies in 1950 got to 30-100).

JJ Wetherholt, Cardinals: Defensive metrics love Wetherholt and help push him to 4.5 WAR in 139 games. He hit .242/.339/.365 with 17 homers, 14 steals and 89 runs.

Jhoan Duran, Phillies: In his first full season with the Phillies, Duran closed down 33 of his 35 save chances with a 1.82 ERA, 0.99 WHIP and 84 strikeouts in 59 ⅓ innings.

Mason Miller, Padres: In 70 innings across 66 appearances, Miller pitched to a 1.67 ERA, 0.90 WHIP and struck out 129 hitters. He won five games and converted 38 of his 41 save chances.

Trevor Megill, Brewers: Though the Brewers didn't always employ a traditional closer, Megill was the closest thing to it, securing 30 saves in 33 chances with a 2.63 ERA, 0.89 WHIP and 69 strikeouts in 61 2/3 innings.

Don Mattingly, Phillies: Mattingly started the season as the bench coach before taking over a 9-19 team for the fired Rob Thomson. Immediately, the Phillies got hot. They ended up going 79-55 under Mattingly, making the playoffs yet again despite starting 10 games under .500.

Pat Murphy, Brewers: Managers almost never win this award in back-to-back seasons because it's generally given to the guy whose team most exceeded expectations. How could that possibly happen two straight years? Well, Murphy now is going for three. In 2025, the Brewers set a franchise record with 97 wins and had the best record in baseball. In 2026, they set a franchise record with 103 wins and had the best record in baseball.

Walt Weiss, Braves: In 2025, the final season of Brian Snitker's career, the Braves were a disappointing 76-86. Weiss was hired in the offseason and went 94-68, getting the Braves back on top in the NL East after a two-year hiatus.

#2661. Robinson Canó Jr., son of eight-time MLB All-Star, agrees to $1 million deal with Marlins, per reports

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Miami Marlins have reached a preliminary agreement with 16-year-old Robinson Canó Jr. that stands to make him part of the club's 2028 international signing class. The agreement is worth $1 million, reports Mike Rodriguez.

MLB rules state that an international amateur free agent player is eligible to sign with an MLB organization between Jan. 15 and Dec. 15 of his signing class year. He must turn 17 before Sept. 1 of the year in which he signs.

Canó Jr., a highly regarded shortstop out of the Dominican Republic who bats right-handed, is the son of former MLB great Robinson Canó. The elder Canó spent parts of 17 seasons in the majors, the majority of which came with the New York Yankees. Over that span, Canó earned eight All-Star selections and three Gold Gloves; racked up 2,639 hits and 335 home runs; and won a World Series ring as a member of the 2009 Yankees. He went on to sign a large free-agent contract with the Seattle Mariners, where he played from 2014-18.

Canó's career total of 68.7 WAR would under normal circumstances make him a strong candidate for election to the Baseball Hall of Fame. However, two suspensions for positive PED tests make it unlikely he'll get a plaque, at least while he's on the BBWAA ballot. He last appeared in the majors in 2022 as a member of the Atlanta Braves.

Canó Jr. is also the grandson of José Canó, who appeared in the majors with the 1989 Houston Astros, which puts him in line to be a third-generation major leaguer.

#2659. Andreeva wins 11 games in a row to thrash Sabalenka at WTA Finals

Mirra Andreeva won 11 games in a row as she thrashed world number two Aryna Sabalenka to reach the last four at the WTA Finals.

French Open champion Andreeva was 4-1 down in the opening set before producing some superb tennis and taking advantage of an increasingly erratic Sabalenka performance.

The 19-year-old Russian went on to deliver a statement 6-4 6-0 victory over four-time major singles winner Sabalenka.

As poor as Sabalenka was, Andreeva produced a mature, intelligent performance to shut her out of the match.

She used loopy high balls to initially wrong-foot Sabalenka and then showcased her easy power, hitting 16 winners to only six unforced errors and creating brilliant angles from the baseline.

"I will be honest, I feel like Aryna did not have the best day," Andreeva told Sky Sports.

"I feel like I cannot really take all the credit today - I feel like that is not very fair in some ways.

"I'm just happy. I had a goal in front of me to commit no matter what and control the things I can control."

Belarus' Sabalenka, by contrast, hit 23 unforced errors and failed to produce a single ace at Indian Wells.

The second seed had taping on her knee but it did not seem to hinder her - this, rather, was a performance similar to some of the collapses she has had this year.

Just as in the French Open quarter-finals, where she lost the third set 6-0, Sabalenka could not find her rhythm or range.

She won only seven points in the second set as Andreeva breezed to an impressive victory.

The result means the winner of the final group match on Friday between Sabalenka and Elina Svitolina will advance to the semi-finals, while Andreeva goes through as the group winner.

Elina Svitolina won the season-ending WTA Finals in 2019 [Reuters]

Earlier, Svitolina said she "got a bit angry at myself" to inspire a comeback victory over Karolina Muchova and keep her title hopes alive.

Ukraine's Svitolina lost 6-4 6-0 in her first group match against Andreeva on Monday and made an equally poor start against Muchova.

It looked as though things were getting worse for Svitolina when she took a medical timeout for a right hip injury after losing the first set, before finding herself an early break point down.

However, the sixth seed saved it and then gradually wore down Wimbledon runner-up Muchova to win 3-6 6-2 6-2.

Muchova hit 39 unforced errors throughout the match - the majority of which came from her forehand - as Svitolina ground her down.

The Czech could not recover from giving up an early break in the third set and handed over another with her eighth double fault of the match.

Svitolina made no mistake, with the 32-year-old tipping her head back and roaring in celebration after securing the win.

"I was really angry at myself after the first match and the first set," Svitolina told Sky Sports.

"Sometimes it [channelling frustration] happens in a good way and sometimes in a bad way.

"I tried to direct my anger towards the ball and I found my game in the end."

At the Stockholm Open, Britain's Cameron Norrie fell 7-5 6-3 to world number 10 Taylor Fritz.

Denmark's Holger Rune reached the quarter-finals of the tournament, a year after he ruptured his Achilles at the same event.

Rune only made his return to the ATP Tour in October after a gruelling 12 months recovering from the injury, but beat Miomir Kecmanovic 2-6 6-1 6-4 to advance.

#2658. Brewers bash champion Dodgers to brink of NLCS sweep; CBS Sports Preseason All-America team revealed

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

This is an article version of the CBS Sports HQ AM Newsletter, the ultimate guide to every day in sports. You can sign up to get it in your inbox every weekday morning here.

One of the biggest benefits of the NIL era is that college basketball has more elite talent than ever, now that players are returning for bigger paychecks instead of bolting for NBA money at the first opportunity.

That made selecting our 2026-27 CBS Sports Preseason All-America teams especially difficult, but our experts nailed it. Each of the three teams features players who will be performing at the next level very soon, but the best of those might be Florida superstar Thomas Haugh.

As our own Isaac Trotter explains, if Haugh can improve his range shooting, he won't have to wait long to hear his name called in the 2027 NBA Draft.

When it comes to how the talent broke down by conference, it was a a pretty level playing field for the most part.

Not to spoil anyting, but Arizona freshman Caleb Holt did not make the cut. He did, however, turn some heads in the Wildcats' exhibition game.

Loyalty is an excellent quality to have in a friend or partner. It's also why we love dogs.

It should not be quite as prevalent among college football coaches, some of whom have been undone because they did what was comfortable, not what was necessarily best for the team.

Our own John Talty highlighted five high-profile coaches who have been loyal to a fault, making hires and personnel decisions that have come back to haunt them. One of those coaches is Mike Elko. After a shaky season from Marcel Reed in 2025, Texas A&M chose not to pursue an upgrade in the portal.

Instead, the Aggies gave Reed a major payday, and they'll miss the College Football Playoff because of it.

Look, it can happen to the best of us. Dan Lanning and Dabo Swinney wound up on the list, despite the success that those two have had throughout their careers.

Steve Sarkisian is another coach who has fallen into the trap of being too loyal, but he may have a huge decision on his hands in the offseason. Arch Manning has struggled enough that another year in college should be on the table. If that happens, would Sark welcome back Manning with open arms, despite his shortcomings?

Finally, one person for whom loyalty is no an issue is Missouri QB Austin Simmons. After Trinidad Chambliss won the starting job at Ole Miss last year, Simmons didn't feel the need to stick around, but there won't be bitterness when Simmons returns to Oxford this weekend.

#2657. Tarik Skubal contract predictions: Ace's new deal could break multiple MLB records for a pitcher

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Tarik Skubal is about to become a very, very rich man. The two-time Cy Young winner and arguably the best pitcher in baseball hits free agency this winter, and it stands to reason that he'll break the record for highest-paid pitcher in MLB history, both by total value and average annual value.

By total value, Dodgers ace Yoshinobu Yamamoto currently holds that record thanks to the 12-year, $325 million contract he signed ahead of the 2024 season (we're eliminating Shohei Ohtani from the running for obvious reasons, though his 10-year, $700 million deal would clearly lead the list).

As for AAV, Ohtani again tops the class at $70 million a year, but for those who only pitch, Max Scherzer and Justin Verlander share the record at $43.33 million annually.

The expectation is that Skubal will break both records, even as the owners try to tamp down on spending in the ongoing CBA negotiations. Just how high could those figures go? CBS Sports experts pulled out their calculators.

Mike Axisa: Seven years and $325.5 million. That's $46.5 million per season and it would break the records for average annual value (Max Scherzer's and Justin Verlander's $43.3 million) and total guarantee (Yoshinobu Yamamoto's $325 million) for a pitcher. I would expect there to be an opt out because those are just the cost of doing business these days. Maybe even multiple opt outs. Scott Boras loves to break records, though, and this contract allows him to break two.

Dayn Perry: I'll say eight years, $350 million. Likewise, that sets the record for total contract value and AAV for a pitcher. Normally, I'd ding him a bit for those elbow problems in his walk year, but he was mostly dominant after returning ahead of schedule. I also think Skubal will benefit from an aggressive pre-lockout market and from a pretty thin free agent class overall.

Matt Snyder: Eight years, $400 million. This gets him the record deal for pitchers both in terms of the guarantee and the average annual value. I'm probably going too low on the years, but I feel like teams have been burned so many times before on the length of pitcher deals due to injury that this holds down the market a bit. Ever so slightly. I do think there will be opt outs after years three and five.

#2655. Timberwolves Sign Big-Time G-League Scoring Center To Two-Way Deal

A second-round draft pick often needs time to settle into the NBA. Johni Broome's first season took him through the Philadelphia 76ers and their G League affiliate, and a knee injury interrupted his progress. He has already produced at a high level against college and G League competition. What remains uncertain is whether he can earn a regular role against NBA players.

The Minnesota Timberwolves now have a chance to find out. They have agreed to a two-way deal with Broome, giving the former Auburn Tigers standout another opportunity to develop in the league.

Purdue Boilermakers forward Trey Kaufman-Renn (4) goes up for a layup over Auburn Tigers forward Johni Broome (4) as Auburn Tigers take on Purdue Boilermakers at Legacy Arena in Birmingham, Ala., on Saturday, Dec. 21, 2024. Auburn Tigers defeated Purdue Boilermakers 87-69. USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect

Senior NBA insider Mike Scotto reported the agreement. Minnesota created the opening on November 3rd when it waived forward Enrique Freeman. The Timberwolves tried to bring in Norchad Omier, but that effort did not result in a signing. Omier later agreed to a two-way contract with the Cleveland Cavaliers, who officially signed him on November 6th.

Scotto shared the news through his official X account. He wrote, "The Minnesota Timberwolves and Johni Broome have agreed to a two-way deal, league sources told @hoopshype."

Scotto also identified Broome as the 35th pick in the 2025 NBA Draft. He noted Broome's SEC Player of the Year award and his consensus All-American honors.

The report does not include contract terms. It describes an agreement rather than a formal announcement from the Timberwolves.

Even so, Broome's arrival would give Minnesota another young frontcourt player to evaluate without using a standard roster contract.

Broome left Auburn with a strong college record. He averaged 18.6 points and 10.8 rebounds across 36 games in the 2024-25 season. He also handed out 2.9 assists a night and blocked 2.1 shots. He shot 51% from the field and led the SEC in rebounding. He earned SEC Player of the Year and consensus First-Team All-American honors.

He also won the Karl Malone Award and the Pete Newell Big Man Award. Auburn reached its first Final Four since the 2018-19 season with Broome leading the frontcourt.

Those numbers explain why Philadelphia selected him with the 35th pick. Broome could score near the basket and collect rebounds at both ends. He also protected the rim. He was more comfortable passing than many players at his position.

Broome's rookie season showed how hard it can be to turn college success into NBA minutes. He played 11 regular-season games for Philadelphia, where he averaged 0.9 points and 1.5 rebounds in about five minutes a night. Most of his playing time came with the Delaware Blue Coats.

His G League production was much stronger. Broome averaged 21.8 points across 26 appearances for Delaware. He added 8.3 rebounds and 3.2 assists. He also averaged 1.5 blocks. Earlier in February, he recorded a 50-point, 17-rebound game for the Blue Coats. A torn meniscus in his right knee interrupted that run. He underwent surgery in February and missed roughly seven weeks before becoming available for the playoffs.

Philadelphia did not use him in its first-round series against the Boston Celtics. His postseason minutes came only after the second-round series against the New York Knicks turned into a blowout. His path became less settled after the season. Philadelphia traded him to the Los Angeles Clippers in July, and the Clippers, a team criticized for neglecting its young talent, waived him in September.

The Milwaukee Bucks signed him to an Exhibit 10 deal in October before waiving him on October 17th. Minnesota is now his next stop.

Broome's best work comes inside near the basket. He can finish around the rim and score after offensive rebounds. He can also make passes from the post and block shots. Those skills give Minnesota a different type of frontcourt prospect to develop.

His outside shooting needs work. Broome made 28.9% of his three-point attempts in the G League. That could limit how easily he fits beside Rudy Gobert, who also does most of his scoring near the basket. Minnesota already has young centers in Joan Beringer and Rocco Zikarsky. Beringer has already shown signs of growth in a spot start against the Spurs. Broome will have to earn his place in a frontcourt group that has rebounded surprisingly well this season for the Timberwolves.

His passing gives the coaching staff another skill to work with. A big man who can move the ball after receiving it in the post can help keep an offense moving, even when he is not taking the shot. Broome needs to guard NBA players and improve his range. Until he does, that skill set will not earn him consistent minutes.

The Timberwolves have taken a low-risk route with a player whose college and G League results deserve another look. For a team that still must prove it is more than Anthony Edwards, that is a small bet with real upside. Broome's next step is less about scoring 20 points. He must handle NBA defensive assignments and make quicker decisions. He also has to improve his outside shot.

Those changes will decide whether this agreement becomes more than a short stop.

#2654. Bronny James faces uncertain NBA future after Lakers assign him to G League

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Los Angeles Lakers assigned Bronny James and rookie Cameron Carr to the G League on Thursday, the team announced. James is no stranger to the Coachella Valley Lakers, having spent time with them across his first two seasons. Still, such an early G League assignment isn't exactly an encouraging start to his third NBA campaign.

James, the 22-year-old son of LeBron James, played for the Lakers in the playoffs last season out of desperation due injuries, but when the team has been closer to full strength, he has failed to earn more than spot minutes in his first two NBA seasons. He struggled mightily in the preseason this year, as he shot just 4 of 16 from the field. And while he has always been a defense-first player, his size -- 6-foot-2 and 210 pounds -- has limited his upside on that side of the floor.

"I thought he had a really nice September and a good summer with us, but I don't think he's played well in the four preseason games," Lakers coach JJ Redick said in October.

Despite those preseason struggles, James survived final cuts as the Lakers ultimately waived former No. 17 overall pick Dalton Knecht to get their roster down to 15 players. The move was relatively surprising considering their draft status. While both Knecht and James have fallen short of the team's hopes for them, Knecht was a former first-round pick who had at least held a consistent rotation role early in his rookie season. He fell off after a failed trade to the Charlotte Hornets, but teams typically like to give their own first-round picks as many opportunities as possible to succeed.

Knecht has since signed a two-way contract with the defending NBA champion New York Knicks. He appeared in his first game on Wednesday, a blowout win over the Chicago Bulls, and he notched 10 points in 16 minutes. By comparison, James has scored four points in 12 minutes spread across five appearances this season.

James was drafted in 2024 and became the first player in NBA history to share the court with his father. Now the elder James is a member of the Philadelphia 76ers, and both teams are doing well after their separation. The 76ers have the NBA's best record at 8-1, and the Lakers aren't far behind at 7-2. But with his father gone and the Lakers thriving in his absence, the younger James is in a somewhat precarious position moving forward. His name carries less weight with the organization than it once did, and a team with championship ambitions isn't going to be willing to wait on the development of a second-round pick forever.

James' contract is guaranteed through the end of this season, but not guaranteed afterward. If he doesn't show progress quickly, he could be a trade candidate at the deadline or simply not retained after the season.

#2653. Why MLB could see an early free agency frenzy before the potential Dec. 1 lockout

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Most of the season, my assumption was that November would be a slow month for the hot stove. There is a new collective bargaining agreement coming, likely after a lockout, and I figured teams would not want to commit significantly to future payroll without first seeing what the new CBA would bring. Salary cap, stiffer competitive balance tax penalties, whatever.

A perfectly reasonable stance, that is, and I say that as someone who is happy to call out teams and owners who do not appear to be putting forth the best effort to contend, if you catch my drift. My assumption was November would be slow. I am here now to tell you why my assumption not just may be wrong, but likely is wrong, and the hot stove will burn bright in November.

The CBA expires at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1, or four weeks from Tuesday. Here now are four reasons why MLB clubs could be active between now and then.

MLB teams committed more than $1.7 billion to free agents in November 2021, just before the last CBA expired and the owners locked out the players. That includes the Rangers, who spent more than $560 million on Jon Gray, Corey Seager, and Marcus Semien. Those three later helped the Rangers win the franchise's first World Series title in 2023. Five players signed nine-figure contracts in the weeks leading up to the last lockout.

It is not only the teams we must consider here. More than 140 players became free agents the day after the World Series, and you can be sure many (most?) of them would prefer to sign before the lockout. They want to get their contract locked in and know where they'll play next season so they can find a place to live, get the kids enrolled in school, etc. Peace of mind during the lockout will go a long way.

MLB's owners did not propose a salary cap during the last round of labor negotiations, but there was similar uncertainty about what the upcoming CBA would bring, and teams spent lots of money anyway. Past behavior can inform us about what to expect in the future and what we saw leading into the last lockout suggests it will be a busy four weeks.

During the last lockout, MLB amended its posting agreement with Japan's Nippon Professional Baseball league and paused the 45-day negotiating window during the lockout. Seiya Suzuki was posted on Nov. 22, 2021, his 45 days were paused when the lockout began on Dec. 1, then they resumed when the lockout ended on March 10, 2022. Suzuki signed with the Cubs on March 18.

NPB players will not have the same luxury this year. MLB has declined to amend its posting agreement this offseason, according to The Athletic, so NPB players potentially face a hard Dec. 1 signing deadline even though they were officially posted on Nov. 1. They won't get the full 45 days because players cannot sign MLB contracts during the lockout. Their posting window is really 30 days.

This applies to three of our top 50 free agents: Hanshin Tigers third baseman Teruaki Sato (No. 4), Seibu Lions righty Kaima Taira (No. 19), and Hokkaido Nippon Ham Fighters righty Hiromi Itoh (No. 26). All three were posted on Nov. 1 and their 45-day posting window should run through Dec. 16. Instead, they must sign by Dec. 1 with the lockout looming, or return to Japan for 2027.

Tarik Skubal, far and away the best free agent on the market, is expected to sign before the lockout, reports ESPN. There is always a bit of a domino effect with top free agents. Several big spenders (Blue Jays, Cubs, Dodgers, Mets, etc.) are expected to pursue Skubal, and the teams that lose out could quickly pivot to their secondary targets to avoid being left empty-handed.

We saw a good example of this domino effect last offseason. The Dodgers beat out the Mets for Kyle Tucker and agreed to terms with the outfielder on Jan. 16. The Mets quickly pivoted and agreed to a contract with Bo Bichette just a few hours later. They had money to spend and a void in the lineup, and after losing out on their top target, New York quickly pivoted to Plan B.

The sooner Skubal signs, the sooner second-tier free agent starters like Freddy Peralta and Trevor Rogers will come off the board. Teams need pitching, always and forever, and once the best available starter comes off the board, there figures to be a rush to get whoever's left. Skubal is expected to sign before the lockout. Other starters won't be far behind then.

Even if the MLB Players Association relents and agrees to a salary cap, it is unlikely the cap will be fully implemented in 2027. MLB has expressed a willingness to phase in a salary cap over some number of years and, honestly, it's a must. It will be impossible for big payroll clubs like the Dodgers, Mets, and Yankees to trim payroll and get cap-compliant immediately after the lockout.

November may be the last chance for all teams, not just those with deep pockets, to spend freely and have contracts grandfathered into whatever economic system the new CBA brings. Spend now, deal with the consequences later. That kind of thing. It may sound foolish -- the bill will come due eventually, right? -- but rarely is the hot stove league and free agency rational.

"You prepare under the current system, and then you adjust along the way," Blue Jays president Mark Shapiro told Sportsnet last month. "Any new system adopted, there will be a timeframe for adjustment into that system. I don't think any new system adopted would cause for immediate action."

#2651. Mariners hire Cubs executive with no managerial experience as new manager

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

After a colossally disappointing 2026 season, the Seattle Mariners are bringing in a first-time manager. The Mariners have named Chicago Cubs director of player development Jason Kanzler their new manager, the team announced Tuesday. Seattle fired manager Dan Wilson after the season.

"Our goal in this process was finding a manager with the ability to challenge all of us to improve," president of baseball operations Jerry Dipoto said in a statement. "Jason has the mindset, expertise, communication skills, and intensity to help create a championship standard here in Seattle."

The Mariners will be Kanzler's first managerial job at any level. At 36, he will be the second-youngest manager in baseball, older than only 34-year-old Washington Nationals skipper Blake Butera.

Bringing in a manager with zero previous managerial experience at any level is a rare move, certainly, though it is not unprecedented. Most notably, the New York Yankees hired Aaron Boone straight from the broadcasting booth in 2018. Boone had no managerial or coaching experience at any level. He's led the Yankees to the postseason eight times in nine seasons.

"I am thrilled to join the Mariners organization and I'm looking forward to hitting the ground running," Kanzler said in a statement. "This team has an immense amount of talent in all facets of the game, and my coaching staff and I are excited to access and unlock this team's full potential."

Kanzler may have no prior managerial experience, but this will not be his first time on a big-league staff. He was a major-league coach with the Houston Astros in 2022 and their assistant hitting coach in 2023, and had coached in their farm system previously. The Cubs hired Kanzler to oversee their player development in 2024.

Former Astros manager Joe Espada was reportedly the other finalist for the Mariners job.

The Mariners went 76-86 this past season and finished five games back in the woebegone AL West. A year ago, they went to Game 7 of the ALCS and were five outs away from their first-ever trip to the World Series. Seattle entered 2026 as a trendy World Series pick and instead fell flat, mostly because so many core hitters underperformed.

Kanzler will be the team's third manager since Dipoto was hired to run baseball operations in September 2015, joining Scott Servais (2015-24) and Wilson (2024-26).

#2649. Former actor, current driver Frankie Muniz hospitalized after incident before Wednesday's Ford exhibition race

Frankie Muniz was hospitalized Wednesday after crashing during practice before an exhibition race.

His racing team, Team Reaume, released a statement confirming that he had been taken to a medical facility for further evaluation. The statement noted that the former actor is awake and alert.

Muniz began racing in 2023 in the lower ARCA series. Last year was his first full season as a driver for Team Reaume in the Craftsman Truck Series. He has seven top-20 finishes over his two seasons, four of which came this year.

Wednesday is Ford's "Proud To Honor Veterans Day Classic" exhibition event at the Daytona International Speedway. This is the first iteration of the event, and it was supposed to feature 12 drivers paired into six teams, with each team representing a branch of the military.

Muniz was supposed to be on a team with Cup Series driver Austin Cindric representing the Air Force. Instead, Jenson Altzman will take his spot.

The practice was not open to the public, so it is unclear exactly what happened with Muniz. The race is scheduled to begin at 8 p.m. ET and will be broadcast on USA.

Other drivers competing in the exhibition race include Brad Keselowski, Joey Logano, Noah Gragson, Layne Riggs and Ryan Preece. Drivers will be driving Mustang Dark Horse Rs. Notably, Mustang's Dark Horse SC will be used in the Cup Series next year.

Before getting into racing, Muniz was famous as a child actor. His most recognizable role was Malcolm in the sitcom "Malcolm in the Middle."

He also starred in movies including "Agent Cody Banks," "Big Fat Liar," "My Dog Skip" and "Walk Hard: The Dewey Cox Story."

#2648. NHL Power Rankings: Bruins, Jeremy Swayman off to a roaring start in a tough Atlantic Division

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

You can't make the playoffs in 10 games, but you can definitely give yourself some breathing room when the inevitable ebbs and flows of the season strike. That's exactly what the Boston Bruins have done as they've stood out for the right reasons in a deep Atlantic Division.

Boston currently leads the division with 15 points, and while the Tampa Bay Lightning's record is technically better, the Bruins' plus-14 goal differential is tied for second in the NHL.

The biggest reason for this fast start has been the play of Jeremy Swayman in goal. He's allowed one or fewer goals in half of his starts, and Swayman's 8.02 goals saved above average ranks second to old Beantown running mate Linus Ullmark, per Natural Stat Trick.

We have a long way to go before we start discussing Vezina Trophy candidates seriously, but Swayman certainly has the potential to carry Boston to the postseason.

It helps that David Pastrnak is an elite playmaker, and the Bruins have been getting contributions from young forwards Fraser Minten and James Hagens. Morgan Geekie has also gone from goal-scoring machine to distributor with seven assists in 10 games.

The Atlantic Division will be a heavyweight brawl throughout the season, but to this point, the Bruins have proven to be a worthy combatant. With that in mind, here are the updated NHL Power Rankings.
